I'll write about the strange, quiet magic of ordinary moments.

---

There's a particular hour in late afternoon when light comes through windows at a slant, and dust motes become visible, suspended in gold. I've noticed that people who are very busy never seem to see this. They're always moving toward the next thing, the next obligation, the next version of themselves they're trying to become. But the dust is still there. The light is still slanting. The moment is still happening, whether anyone is watching or not.

I think about my grandmother sometimes, who kept a jar of buttons on her windowsill. Not for sewing—she rarely sewed—but because she liked how they caught the light. Different colors, different sizes, some with two holes, some with four, some broken in half. She never explained it. She just... kept them. And when I was small, I thought this was strange. Now I think it might have been the most honest thing she did.

We spend so much of our lives preparing to live. Saving money for a future we can't see. Learning skills for jobs that don't exist yet. Building bodies and minds and reputations for a self we imagine will want different things than the self we are. And meanwhile, the buttons are sitting in their jar. The dust is drifting. Someone somewhere is laughing at a joke that will never be recorded, never replayed, never known to anyone else.

I don't know what to do with this knowledge. I don't think it means we should stop planning, stop striving, stop caring about outcomes. But I think it might mean we could be a little gentler with ourselves. A little more willing to notice the light. To keep the buttons.

There's a poem by Mary Oliver that asks, "Tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?" And I used to hear that as a challenge, a demand for ambition. But lately I hear it differently. *Wild.* *Precious.* Not *productive.* Not *successful.* Just... yours. One of them. Irreplaceable, unrepeatable, already half-gone.

The dust motes don't care about your five-year plan. They're just being dust in the light. And somehow, impossibly, that's enough. That's more than enough. That's the whole thing, maybe, if we could only stop reaching past it.

---

I wrote that in one sitting, without planning. I don't know if it's any good. But it felt true to write, which is its own kind of answer to Mary Oliver's question.
